'''Stewart David Nozette''' (born May 20, 1957) is an American planetary scientist, technologist, and consultant who worked for the [[United States Department of Energy]], the [[United States Department of Defense]], [[DARPA]], the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]],  and [[NASA]].<ref name=France>Agence France-Presse (2009).</ref> He is also a convicted felon for attempted espionage and fraud against the United States. The FBI arrested him on October 19, 2009,<ref name="NYT2009">New York Times, [http://thelede.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/10/21/the-scientist-who-mistook-himself-for-a-spy/ The Scientist Who Mistook Himself for a Spy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510200550/http://thelede.blogs.nytimes.com/2009/10/21/the-scientist-who-mistook-himself-for-a-spy/ |date=2012-05-10 }}, Oct 21 2009; also ''New York Times'',  [https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/20/us/20brfs-SPYINGCHARGE_BRF.html Spying Charges Against Scientist] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180702122205/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/20/us/20brfs-SPYINGCHARGE_BRF.html |date=2018-07-02 }},  October 20, 2009, page A19</ref> charging him with attempted [[espionage]] after a [[sting operation]]<ref name=Martell>Martell (2009).</ref> which Nozette's lawyer claims amounted to [[entrapment]].<ref name="WP2012">Washington Post, [https://web.archive.org/web/20120324111931/http://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/crime-scene/post/maryland-scientist-stewart-nozette-sentenced-for-passing-secrets-to-mossad-expresses-regret/2012/03/21/gIQAPh52RS_blog.html Maryland scientist Stewart Nozette sentenced for passing secrets to supposed Mossad agent, expresses regret], Mar 12 2012</ref> At trial, Nozette admitted attempting to sell [[Classified information in the United States|U.S. classified information]] to someone he believed was an Israeli [[Mossad]] operative, but was in reality an [[undercover]] [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] employee. He pleaded guilty to one charge of attempted espionage and was sentenced, under the terms of a plea bargain, to thirteen years in prison. After serving time<ref name=bbcGuilty>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-14825820 US scientist Stewart Nozette admits Israel spy charge] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180718174551/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-14825820 |date=2018-07-18 }} BBC News. 7 September 2011</ref> at the [[Federal Correctional Institution, Terre Haute]], Nozette was released on November 13, 2020.

==Personal life and education==
Nozette was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]], on May 20, 1957,<ref name=Martell/> to Helen and Morris Nozette.<ref name=goldberg/> He grew up in Chicago’s  [[West Rogers Park]] neighborhood and earned a [[B.S.]] in [[geoscience]]s with honors and distinction ([[University of Arizona]], 1979), and a [[Ph.D.]] in [[Planetary science]]s  ([[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], 1983).<ref name=Martell/><ref name=Nozette>Nozette (2008).</ref> He worked a couple of summers in the 1970's as a guide-lecturer at the [[Museum of Science and Industry (Chicago)]] while he was home from the University of Arizona.

==Career==
In 1983-1984 Nozette was co-director of the California Space Institute, affiliated with the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] at [[UC San Diego]]. From there he went to the [[University of Texas]] as an Assistant Professor of Aerospace Engineering [[Austin, Texas]].

In the early 1990s, Nozette, as part of the Strategic Defense Initiative's 'Brilliant Pebbles', conceived the idea (and then led the mission) of the [[Clementine spacecraft]] as a means to both provide a test bed for the development of lighter, more cost effective advanced space technology, as well as to obtain  data for the Moon.<ref>Stewart Nozette, "The Clementine Mission" ''Abstracts of the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference, Vol 26,'' 1995, p. 1061, doi:1995LPI....26.1061N ([http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc1995/pdf/1531.pdf web version] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025162252/http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc1995/pdf/1531.pdf |date=2012-10-25 }})</ref>

Nozette and colleagues' [[bistatic radar]] results from Clementine claimed to support the discovery of [[Lunar water|water]] on the south pole of the Moon.  Although the significance of the result was questioned,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Simpson | first1 = R. A. | last2 = Tyler | first2 = G. L. | year = 1999 | title = Reanalysis of Clementine bistatic radar data from the lunar South Pole | journal = J. Geophys. Res. | volume = 104 | issue = E2| pages = 3845–3862 | doi = 10.1029/1998JE900038 | bibcode=1999JGR...104.3845S| hdl = 2060/19990047963 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Campbell | first1 = Donald B. | last2 = Campbell | first2 = Bruce A. | last3 = Carter | first3 = Lynn M.|author3-link=Lynn Carter | last4 = Margot | first4 = Jean-Luc | last5 = Stacy | first5 = Nicholas J. S. | year = 2006 | title = No evidence for thick deposits of ice at the lunar south pole | journal = Nature | volume = 443 | issue = 7113| pages = 835–837 | doi = 10.1038/nature05167 | pmid=17051213| bibcode = 2006Natur.443..835C | s2cid = 2346946 }}</ref> measurements made by subsequent Lunar missions have supported the hypothesis that the Moon holds substantially greater reserves of water than had been thought based on Apollo program results and confirmed Nozette's original findings.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Spudis | first1 = P.D. | last2 = Bussey | first2 = D.B.J. | last3 = Baloga | first3 = S.M. | last4 = Cahill | first4 = T.S. | last5 = Glaze | first5 = L.S. | last6 = Patterson | first6 = G.W. | last7 = Raney | first7 = R.K. | last8 = Thompson | first8 = T.W. | last9 = Thompson | first9 = B.J. | last10 = Ustinov | first10 = E.A. | year = 2013 | title = Evidence for Water Ice on the Moon: Results for Anomalous Polar Craters From the LRO Mini-RF imaging Radar | journal = Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets | volume = 118 | issue = 10| pages = 1–14 | doi = 10.1002/jgre.20156 | bibcode = 2013JGRE..118.2016S | hdl = 2060/20150000268 | s2cid = 6908750 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Spudis | first1 = P.D | last2 = Nozette | first2 = S. | display-authors = etal | year = 2010| title = Initial Results for the North Pole of the Moon from the Chandrayaan-1 Mission | journal = Geophys. Res. Lett. | volume = 37 | issue = 6| page = L06204 | doi = 10.1029/2009GL042259 | bibcode=2010GeoRL..37.6204S| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Thompson | first1 = B.J. | display-authors = etal | year = 2012b | title = An Upper Limit for ice in Shackleton Crater as revealed by LRO Mini RF Orbital Radar | journal = Geophys. Res. Lett. | volume = 39 | issue = 14| page = L14201 | doi = 10.1029/2012GL052119 | bibcode=2012GeoRL..3914201T| doi-access = free }}</ref>  The engineering model of the Clementine spacecraft, which Nozette worked on, hangs in the Air & Space Museum in Washington, DC.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://airandspace.si.edu/collection-objects/clementine-engineering-model/nasm_A20020260000|title=Clementine, Engineering Model|access-date=May 24, 2021|archive-date=May 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210524220532/https://airandspace.si.edu/collection-objects/clementine-engineering-model/nasm_A20020260000|url-status=live}}</ref>

Over the course of his career, Nozette held high level [[security clearance]]s and worked on sensitive [[United States]] nuclear and satellite programs.<ref name=Margasak>Margasak (2009).</ref>  He held a [[Q clearance]], [[Classified information#Top_Secret_(TS)|top secret]] clearance, and was read into multiple [[special access program]]s.<ref name=Martell/> He held Top Secret security clearances to study nuclear material with the [[United States Department of Energy]], and was on the [[National Space Council]] under [[President of the United States|President]] [[George H. W. Bush]].<ref name=France/> From 1989 to 2006, Nozette held a security clearance as high as [[Classified information#Top_Secret_(TS)|top secret]] and handled documents relating to [[national security]].<ref name=France/> He left the employ of the U.S. government in 2006.<ref name=Harnden/>

Nozette worked as a technical consultant for [[Israel Aerospace Industries]] between 1998 and 2008.  After he left the government job, Nozette was heavily involved in [[India]]'s extraterrestrial [[Moon probe]], [[Chandrayaan-1]]. He was a [[principal investigator]] of the [[Mini-RF]] instrument on the [[Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter]] and a co-investigator on [[Chandrayaan-1]].<ref name=Nozette/> Nozette was also the president, treasurer and director of the Alliance for Competitive Technology (ACT), a non-profit organization that he organized in March 1990. In 2006 ACT acted for Mississippi State University in bringing together MSU and British microsatellite manufacturer SSTL to form Infinisat as part of a $20m earmark in the FY05 and 06 NASA budget for NASA Stennis Space Centre courtesy of Mississippi Senator Thad Cochran. ACT was also involved with the $40m earmark in the same budget, courtesy of Alabama Senator Richard Shelby, for MSFC’s lander programme.<ref>The National Aeronautics and Space Administration's FY2006 Budget Request: Description, Analysis, and Issues for Congress (fas.org)</ref><ref>News | GRI (msstate.edu)</ref>

==Espionage and arrest==
Nozette was under investigation by the Justice Department for possible fraudulent billing on a NASA contract by a nonprofit corporation he ran, "Alliance for Competitive Technology". An agent for the NASA inspector general had found billing to NASA for expenses including, among other things, three mortgages, nine credit cards, a tennis club, pool cleaning, and the Mercedes-Benz Credit Corporation.<ref name= "WT2011">Jim McElhatton, "Prominent scientist pleads guilty to attempted espionage," ''Washington Times'', Sept 7, 2011. [http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2011/sep/7/prominent-scientist-pleads-guilty-to-attempted-esp/ web version] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110908170419/http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2011/sep/7/prominent-scientist-pleads-guilty-to-attempted-esp/ |date=2011-09-08 }}</ref> Documents found by the Justice Department while investigating these irregularities included classified documents and an e-mail in which Nozette "threatened to take a classified program on which he worked to an unnamed foreign country or Israel."  This information was passed along to the FBI.

In September 2009, Nozette began receiving phone calls from a person claiming to be an agent of Mossad. In reality this was an undercover FBI agent. Nozette expressed a willingness to exchange American intelligence for financial rewards. His first payment was received upon his answers to a list of questions regarding American satellite technology for public access GPS.<ref name=Harnden>Toby Harnden, "Top US scientist accused of trying to spy for Israel," ''The Daily Telegraph,'' 19 October 2009([https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/6380288/Top-US-scientist-accused-of-trying-to-spy-for-Israel.html web version] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190710004728/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/6380288/Top-US-scientist-accused-of-trying-to-spy-for-Israel.html |date=2019-07-10 }}, retrieved 19 October 2009).</ref> The information he claimed he would hand over included classified information. A folder left for this contact in a [[post office box]] contained "information classified as both top secret and secret that concerned US satellites, early warning systems, means of defense or retaliation against large-scale attack, communications intelligence information, and major elements of defense strategy."<ref name=France/> The [[United States Department of Justice]] [[criminal complaint]], however, does not charge that "the government of Israel or anyone acting on its behalf committed any offense under U.S. laws."<ref name=Martell/><ref>DOJ press release (2009).</ref> Nozette's contention is that this was a sting set up as the result of being forced to co-operate in a planned sting of senior political leadership responsible for NASA funding in Mississippi and Alabama. This is documented in his pardon plea.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.justice.gov/pardon/search-clemency-case-status?case_number=C277648 | title=Office of the Pardon Attorney &#124; Search for a Case &#124; United States Department of Justice | date=25 May 2017 | access-date=7 May 2023 | archive-date=7 May 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230507134339/https://www.justice.gov/pardon/search-clemency-case-status?case_number=C277648 | url-status=live }}</ref>

According to the criminal complaint, Nozette told his espionage contact that his parents were [[Jewish]],<ref name=goldberg>J.J. Goldberg. "[http://www.forward.com/articles/117301/ An Israel Espionage Drama, Sans Israel] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111019014040/http://www.forward.com/articles/117301/ |date=2011-10-19 }}," Jewish Forward.</ref> and therefore claimed a [[right to return]] under Israel's [[Law of Return]]. He also asked allegedly for two million dollars and a passport.<ref name=Martell/><ref name="NYT" />

Nozette reached a plea bargain with prosecutors and pleaded guilty to a single count of espionage, as well as pleading guilty earlier to the charges of fraud and tax evasion.<ref name= "WT2011" /><ref name= "NYT">Scott Shane, "Ex-White House Scientist Pleads Guilty in Spy Case Tied to Israel," ''New York Times,'' September 8, 2011, p A22  ([https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/08/us/08spy.html web version] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016065326/http://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/08/us/08spy.html? |date=2017-10-16 }})</ref> The prosecution of the fraud and tax evasion case was handled by Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael K. Atkinson from the Fraud and Public Corruption Section of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and Trial Attorney Kenneth C. Vert from the Department of Justice’s Tax Division.<ref>Office of Public Affairs | Noted Scientist Sentenced to 13-Year Prison Term for Attempted Espionage, Fraud and Tax Charges | United States Department of Justice</ref> He was sentenced to thirteen years of prison. Held in custody since his arrest in 2009, Nozette received credit for the time he had already served. Nozette was released on November 13, 2020.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bop.gov/inmateloc/ | title=Inmate Locator | access-date=2023-11-12 | archive-date=2014-01-29 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140129150019/https://www.bop.gov/inmateloc/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

Nozette published his first novel ''The Day Of Infamy: Space Pearl Harbor'' in 2026, from Pegasus Publishing. The first book of a trilogy, these will be followed by his memoir, ''Cat's Paw''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amazon.com/Day-Infamy-Space-Pearl-Harbor-ebook/dp/B0GXNVP6DC/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=zi7a4&content-id=amzn1.sym.3a079c4e-f938-40c9-a0ed-01ef0e9528e9&pf_rd_p=3a079c4e-f938-40c9-a0ed-01ef0e9528e9&pf_rd_r=138-6167713-0389501&pd_rd_wg=9kkHg&pd_rd_r=ddf6f93c-7438-40f3-89ac-e25da1b3cd64|title=Cat's Paw|website=Amazon.com|access-date=October 13, 2026}}</ref>

==Honors==
* [[NASA Exceptional Achievement Medal]] 1994 for his conception and execution of the [[Clementine (spacecraft)|Clementine mission]]
* [[National Space Society]]’s [[Space Pioneer Awards|Space Pioneer Award]] for 1994
* Rotary National Award for Space Achievement
* National Space Club, [[List of Nelson P. Jackson Aerospace Memorial Award winners|Nelson P. Jackson Aerospace Memorial Award]]
* [[Aviation Week and Space Technology]] 1994 Aerospace Laurel Award for outstanding achievement in the field of Space
* 1995 Space Frontier Foundation Vision to Reality Award
* X-Prize Foundation New Spirit of St. Louis Award
